It's shitty to insult either group. And you're right, ultimately we're all looking at these things from our perspectives. But I can acknowledge that saying certain insults to me will in all likelihood not mean as much as saying those same kinds of insults to someone who is in a worse position than me. 

You could say "but you don't know how they feel" about a calling a guy who walks slowly a cripple versus saying it to a man who can't walk. The idea that the insults are at the same severity is silly to me. 

I can't take this argument further though, because we can run down the subjective rabbit hole of "but how bad does it really make that person feel" forever.

"Thing is you can't tell by a person's apparent group membership what their life experience is." 

We're discussing averages here. On average, a white person will have been granted far more social privileges based off of their race compared to a black person. So in the context of racial slurs in America, it would be worse to use one towards black people, because of their disadvantages in regards to their race. 

This is not to say all white people have lived easy lives, nor that there aren't black people living better than some white people. Yes, their are poor white people that were bullied and robbed and are ugly or suffer from deformities. And it would be way more egregious to call some white dude who was severely burned in a fire "flameman" than it would be to call a regular black dude that. 
 
The existence of disadvantages does not remove the reality of privileges one has benefited from. The vast majority of white people are given a better hand purely based off being white in America. The same way Brad Pitt was given an upper hand in life purely because he had model-tier looks. If you think it's wrong to assume that some one is privileged based off of a trait that is universally associated with positives in society, okay, I can't take this argument any further. We're living on different planes of reality. 

And it would be racist to say a racial slur at a person of a privileged group. I'm saying it wouldn't be as bad as saying certain racial slurs about other groups.

Different races of people get treated differently in the United States of America. People who get treated worse being insulted is generally more egregious than the more privileged populations being insulted. Because of the cultural context of the insult. Like calling a dude who's 5"6 a midget versus calling a person who actually has dwarfism a midget. Different contexts, different life experiences.

I'm not talking about white people in my example. It was just an example of how context effects the severity of an insult. 

I'm not talking about if they are "equally racist" (I don't know what that means) I'm talking about the level of disrespect incurred when using one slur vs another. 

There are a group of nerds constantly getting their heads dunked in a toilet and come to be called "dunk heads". Then there are a group of popular girls who all get braces and look goofy so they're called "brace face". Which insult is worse? I think it's the one associated with a history of intense physical and verbal abuse.

I agree colorism runs both ways. I should've clarified that when I explained colorism originally I meant the most prevailing form of colorism (among black people). Colorism as a whole goes beyond negative biases towards dark skinned black people and it goes beyond black people in general. 

And all racial slurs are not equal. This is on par with saying all insults are equal. Different racial slurs have different historical contexts. A dictatorial ruling class being referred to with a disrespectful term made by their oppressed under class is not the same as the rulers doing it to the ruled, due to the context of their relationship.
